interview_metadata.name: Stanley Bates
interview_metadata.protocol: American Voices Project (Park et al. 2024, Table 7) — Full 109 questions

transcript.question_text: To start, I would like to begin with a big question: tell me the story of your life. Start from the beginning -- from your childhood, to education, to family and relationships, and to any major life events you may have had.
transcript.response: I was born in Royal Oak and grew up mostly around the suburban Detroit area, in Troy by the time I was in high school. My dad worked in automotive manufacturing, mostly plant operations and quality control, and my mom taught elementary school, so our house had this mix of practical shop-floor problem solving and school-night structure. I was the kid taking apart radios, trying to make the family computer do things it probably was not meant to do, and then needing my dad to help me put something back together before dinner. I went to Michigan State and got a bachelor's in computer information systems. After college I came back to metro Detroit, started in help desk and junior systems work, and gradually moved into systems analysis, enterprise architecture, cloud work, automation, and incident response. I married Megan in my late twenties; she works in education as a school counselor, and we have two kids, Evan and Claire. The big threads in my life have been technology, family, Detroit sports, cars, and trying to be useful without making everything more dramatic than it needs to be. We live in Bloomfield Hills now, and while it is a comfortable place, I still think of myself as very much a suburban Detroit guy shaped by manufacturing families, public schools, snow tires, and people who expect you to show up when you said you would.

follow_ups.question: What are some concrete memories from your childhood that still feel important to you?
follow_ups.response: Saturday mornings with my dad stand out. He would be in the garage changing oil or checking brakes, and I would hand him tools and ask too many questions. My mom's classroom also mattered; I helped her carry boxes before the school year, and I saw how much work went into helping kids who were all different.

follow_ups.question: When did computers become more than just a hobby for you?
follow_ups.response: Probably around ninth or tenth grade, when I realized I liked figuring out systems more than just playing games on them. I built a basic database for tracking baseball cards, and later I helped a neighbor clean up a small business PC. That was the first time I saw tech as something practical.

follow_ups.question: Who were the central people in your early adulthood?
follow_ups.response: My parents, a couple of college friends from MSU, and Megan after we met through mutual friends in Royal Oak. I had a small circle, not a huge one, but they were steady people. A few of those friendships are still alive through board-game nights and group texts.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us that they've reached a crossroads at some points in their life where multiple paths were available, and their choice then made a significant difference in defining who they are. What about you? Was there a moment like that for you, and if so, could you tell me the whole story about that from start to finish?
transcript.response: The biggest crossroads was about ten years into my career. I had a chance to move into a pure management track at a larger firm, which would have meant more money and a title, or stay closer to architecture and operations at a company where I could still be hands-on. I remember sitting in my Mustang, which was half-restored at the time, outside a coffee shop in Birmingham with a notebook, listing what I actually enjoyed. I liked leading people in a crisis and helping teams make good decisions, but I did not want to become someone who only moved boxes on an org chart. I chose the technical leadership path, and that shaped me. It let me become the person people call during a system outage, but also the person who can explain to finance why a cloud bill is doing what it is doing. It probably delayed a director title, but it kept me credible and curious.

follow_ups.question: Who did you talk to while you were making that decision?
follow_ups.response: Megan, mostly. She asked whether I was chasing the job title or the work itself. I also talked with an older architect named Paul, who told me that credibility compounds if you keep solving real problems.

follow_ups.question: What did that choice change in your day-to-day life?
follow_ups.response: It meant I stayed in design reviews, outage calls, vendor evaluations, and migrations instead of spending all day on budgets and personnel issues. I still led projects, but I kept enough technical depth to be useful when things got messy.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us they made a conscious choice or decision in moments like these, while others say it 'just happened'. What about you?
transcript.response: That one was conscious. I am not always organized about little things, like dentist appointments or bringing the right coupon to the hardware store, but big career decisions get spreadsheets and long walks.

follow_ups.question: What did you weigh most heavily?
follow_ups.response: Whether the job would keep me learning and whether it would still let me be home enough for the kids. Money mattered, but it was not the only column.

follow_ups.question: Did you feel confident afterward?
follow_ups.response: Not immediately. For a few months I wondered if I had passed up the obvious move. Then a major outage happened and I realized I was exactly where I could contribute.

transcript.question_text: Do you think another person or an organization could have lent a helping hand during moments like this?
transcript.response: A more formal mentoring program would have helped. In tech, a lot of career advice is informal, and if you do not happen to know the right senior people, you can drift.

follow_ups.question: What kind of help would have been useful?
follow_ups.response: Someone mapping the difference between management, architecture, product, and consulting tracks in plain English. I had to piece that together through coffee chats.

follow_ups.question: Has that influenced how you mentor others?
follow_ups.response: Yes. I try to tell younger analysts what each path actually looks like on a Tuesday afternoon, not just what the job title sounds like.

transcript.question_text: Moving to present time, tell me more about family who are important to you. Do you have a partner, or children?
transcript.response: I am married to Megan. We have been married about nineteen years, and she is a school counselor, so she brings a lot of emotional intelligence into the house that balances my systems-and-process brain. Our son Evan is sixteen, into robotics, soccer, and music in a casual way. Our daughter Claire is thirteen, likes art, photography, and volleyball, and she is sharper than I was at her age. My parents are still in the area, though they are slowing down; my dad is retired from automotive manufacturing and my mom is retired from teaching. Megan's family is mostly in Michigan too, so holidays are a lot of local driving rather than flights. Family life is busy but not chaotic most of the time. Dinner together happens maybe four nights a week, and Sundays are usually the day where I either ride with the cycling club early or make a bigger meal later.

follow_ups.question: What does a normal evening with your family look like?
follow_ups.response: I get home or shut the laptop around 6:00 or 6:30 unless there is an incident. Megan and I divide dinner, homework checks, rides to practice, and the usual house stuff. Later we might watch a Tigers game, clean the kitchen, or I disappear to the garage for forty minutes.

follow_ups.question: How do you and Megan divide responsibilities?
follow_ups.response: She is better with school calendars and appointments. I handle bills, tech, house maintenance, and most of the weekend cooking. We both do kid transportation depending on whose workday is less locked down.

follow_ups.question: How often do you see your parents?
follow_ups.response: Usually every other week, sometimes weekly if something needs fixing or they need help with a phone, printer, or medical portal. They live close enough that it is not a major production.

transcript.question_text: Are there anyone else in your immediate family whom you have not mentioned? Who are they, and what is your relationship with them like?
transcript.response: I have one younger sister, Laura, who lives in Ann Arbor. We get along well, though we are both busy, so it is texts, holidays, and occasional Saturday lunches.

follow_ups.question: What does Laura do?
follow_ups.response: She works in communications for a nonprofit connected to education. She got more of my mom's public-service gene.

follow_ups.question: Do your families spend time together?
follow_ups.response: A few times a year, especially birthdays and Thanksgiving. Her kids are younger than mine, so the cousins are not in the exact same stage.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anyone else in your life we haven't discussed (like friends or romantic partners). Are there people outside of your family who are important to you?
transcript.response: I have a core friend group from college and work that has stuck around. Dave and Priya come over for board games, usually Terraforming Mars or Ticket to Ride if we are keeping it lighter. I ride some Sundays with people from the Oakland County Cycling Club, and I have a couple of golf buddies at Bloomfield Hills Masters Golf Club. Work friendships matter too, especially the people you have been on 2:00 a.m. incident calls with. You learn pretty quickly who stays calm and who just adds noise.

follow_ups.question: How often do you see friends socially?
follow_ups.response: Board games happen about once a month, golf maybe twice a month in season, and cycling on Sundays when weather and family schedules cooperate.

follow_ups.question: Who would you call if something went wrong?
follow_ups.response: Megan first, then probably Dave for practical help. At work, I would call Anika, our cloud engineering lead, because she is calm and direct.

transcript.question_text: Now let's talk about your current neighborhood. Tell me all about the neighborhood and area in which you are living now.
transcript.response: We live in Bloomfield Hills, which is quiet, leafy, and honestly very fortunate. There are mature trees, larger lots, good schools, and neighbors who keep to themselves but show up when something local needs attention. It is not a walk-to-everything kind of place, so you drive for groceries, sports practices, and restaurants. We are close enough to Detroit that I can get to the DIA, a Tigers game, or a concert without making a whole weekend out of it. The local library is strong, and I have helped with tech literacy events there. It can feel a little insulated, but I appreciate the calm and the schools.

follow_ups.question: Do you know your neighbors well?
follow_ups.response: A few, yes. We talk during snowstorms, yard work, and school events. It is friendly but not everyone-on-the-porch-every-night friendly.

follow_ups.question: Where do you go most often nearby?
follow_ups.response: The library, grocery stores around Birmingham and Bloomfield, the kids' schools, and parks or trails when I want to take photos.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they feel really safe in their neighborhoods, others not so much. How about for you?
transcript.response: I feel very safe. We lock doors and use common sense, but I do not worry much walking around or having the kids outside.

follow_ups.question: Has anything happened nearby that changed that feeling?
follow_ups.response: Mostly minor property stuff, like car break-ins if someone leaves a door unlocked. Nothing that made me feel unsafe day to day.

follow_ups.question: Do you use home security?
follow_ups.response: Yes, partly because I am a tech person. We have cameras, smart locks, and sensors, but I try not to turn the house into a bunker.

transcript.question_text: Living any place has its ups and downs. Tell me about what it's been like for you living here.
transcript.response: The ups are schools, safety, quiet, and access to culture and parks. The downs are cost, property taxes, and sometimes a bubble feeling where people forget how different life is ten miles away.

follow_ups.question: What do you mean by a bubble feeling?
follow_ups.response: Conversations can assume everyone has the same resources, same schedules, same college plans for kids. That is not how most people live, including a lot of families I grew up around.

follow_ups.question: What keeps you connected outside the area?
follow_ups.response: Work, Detroit sports, volunteering, and family. I am in Detroit and surrounding suburbs enough that Bloomfield is not my whole reference point.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about the people who live with you right now, even people who are staying here temporarily.
transcript.response: It is me, Megan, Evan, and Claire. No one else lives with us. The house is busy because teenagers create their own weather systems, but it is a pretty stable household. Evan's robotics parts migrate onto the dining room table if we do not watch it, and Claire's art supplies do the same. Megan and I both work, so we try to keep Sunday evening as the reset time for laundry, calendars, lunches, and making sure nobody has a forgotten form due Monday.

follow_ups.question: Do the kids have their own rooms?
follow_ups.response: Yes, they each have their own room. Evan's is more cables and soccer gear, Claire's is more sketchbooks, photos, and volleyball stuff.

follow_ups.question: Who is home most during weekdays?
follow_ups.response: Usually no one during school hours except me occasionally if I work from home. After school the kids are in and out depending on practices.

transcript.question_text: Is anyone in your household a temporary member, or is everyone a permanent member of the household?
transcript.response: Everyone is a permanent member of the household.

follow_ups.question: No short-term relatives staying right now?
follow_ups.response: No, not right now.

follow_ups.question: Has that happened before?
follow_ups.response: Only for short visits, like holiday weekends.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anyone else who stays here from time to time, if there is anyone like that
transcript.response: My parents or Megan's sister might stay one night around holidays, but nobody regularly.

follow_ups.question: How often would you say overnight guests come?
follow_ups.response: Maybe a handful of times a year.

follow_ups.question: Do the kids have friends sleep over?
follow_ups.response: Occasionally, especially Claire, but it is not every weekend.

transcript.question_text: Is there anyone who usually lives here but is away -- traveling, at school, or in a hospital?
transcript.response: No, everyone who usually lives here is here.

follow_ups.question: No one away at college yet?
follow_ups.response: Not yet. Evan is still in high school.

follow_ups.question: Anyone away for medical care?
follow_ups.response: No.

transcript.question_text: Right now, across a typical week, how do your days vary?
transcript.response: Monday through Friday I am up around 6:15. Coffee first, then I check overnight alerts before the household fully wakes up. I usually work around 8:30 to 5:30, sometimes from home two days a week and in the office the others. Weeknights are dinner, kid logistics, maybe a little garage time or reading if the evening holds together. Saturdays are errands, golf when the weather cooperates, home projects, or photography hikes around Oakland County. Sundays I like to ride with the cycling club early, then cook something bigger, watch Detroit sports, and get ready for the week.

follow_ups.question: What time do you usually go to bed?
follow_ups.response: Around 10:45 or 11:00, unless I get pulled into an incident or start tinkering with something and lose track of time.

follow_ups.question: What part of the week feels most predictable?
follow_ups.response: Weekday mornings. Coffee, alerts, breakfast, school departure, then work. The evenings are more variable because of practices and work issues.

transcript.question_text: At what kind of job or jobs do you work, and when do you work?
transcript.response: I work as a computer systems analyst for a mid-size enterprise services company that supports manufacturing and logistics clients. My job is a blend of requirements analysis, architecture review, cloud migration planning, database and integration work, automation, and incident response. The standard workday is roughly 8:30 to 5:30, Monday through Friday, but systems do not respect calendars. If a production platform goes down, I may be on a call at night or over a weekend. I am not the person typing every command anymore, but I am often the person connecting application, network, cloud, vendor, and business teams so we stop guessing and solve the actual issue.

follow_ups.question: Where do you physically work?
follow_ups.response: A mix. We have an office in the metro Detroit area, and I work from home a couple days a week. For major planning sessions I still prefer being in the room.

follow_ups.question: What tools do you use every day?
follow_ups.response: ServiceNow, Jira, Teams, SQL tools, AWS and Azure consoles, Python scripts, monitoring dashboards, Visio or Lucidchart, and too many spreadsheets.

transcript.question_text: Do you have other routines or responsibilities that you did not already share?
transcript.response: I volunteer with a local STEM after-school program a couple times a month, mostly helping kids with basic coding and robotics concepts. I also help with tech literacy sessions at the Bloomfield Township library, things like password managers, avoiding scams, and setting up cloud backups. At home I handle most of the bills and the home network, which is more elaborate than it probably needs to be. I also try to keep up with my parents' technology and occasional house fixes.

follow_ups.question: When do you volunteer?
follow_ups.response: Usually Wednesday afternoons or early evenings twice a month, depending on the school calendar.

follow_ups.question: What responsibilities do you tend to forget?
follow_ups.response: Appointments and forms. I can remember a server dependency from 2019 but forget that the dentist moved my cleaning to Thursday.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about any recent changes to your daily routine.
transcript.response: The main change is that my work has become more hybrid and more cloud-focused. A few years ago I was commuting almost every day; now I am home two days most weeks, which is good but also makes boundaries fuzzier. Evan getting older changed things too, because he can drive some, so we are not constantly transporting him. Claire's volleyball schedule added different evening pickups. I have also been more intentional about exercise because sitting through architecture meetings all day catches up with you.

follow_ups.question: How has working from home affected family life?
follow_ups.response: It helps with being present for dinner and school pickups, but it also means I can drift back to the laptop too easily after dinner.

follow_ups.question: What exercise did you add?
follow_ups.response: More regular cycling and walking, plus trying to get out for golf instead of calling yard work exercise.

transcript.question_text: If you have children, tell me about a typical weekday during the school year for your children. What is their daily routine? And what are after school activities your children participate in?
transcript.response: Evan is sixteen, so he is up around 6:30, out for high school before 7:30, and after school he has robotics two or three days a week and soccer in season. He does homework at the kitchen island or in his room, depending on how much he needs to focus. Claire is thirteen and starts a little later; she has volleyball practices, art club, and sometimes photography walks with me on weekends. Megan is the master calendar keeper for the school year. I do pickups when work allows and usually handle the late robotics pickup because I am already used to odd hours.

follow_ups.question: Do they eat dinner with you on activity nights?
follow_ups.response: Sometimes it is staggered. We try for family dinner, but during robotics and volleyball season it may be leftovers at 8:15.

follow_ups.question: How involved are you in school activities?
follow_ups.response: I go to games, robotics showcases, conferences, and volunteer when tech help is needed. I am not at every event, but I try to show up for the ones that matter to them.

transcript.question_text: Some people we've talked to tell us about experiences with law enforcement. How about for you?
transcript.response: My personal experiences have been limited and mostly routine. I have had a couple speeding tickets over the years, and once an officer came after a minor fender bender near Woodward. In Bloomfield Hills, police presence is visible but not something I think about every day. I know that is not everyone's experience, and I try to keep that in mind when people talk about policing. I have not had the kind of fearful encounters that some friends and coworkers describe.

follow_ups.question: Have you interacted with police through community events?
follow_ups.response: Yes, mostly school safety nights or local events. Those have been cordial, very suburban, very organized.

follow_ups.question: Do your kids have much contact with law enforcement?
follow_ups.response: Only school resource officer presentations and community events. Nothing personal or serious.

transcript.question_text: What other experiences with law enforcement stand out in your mind?
transcript.response: The main one was when our neighborhood had a rash of unlocked-car thefts. An officer came around reminding people to lock vehicles and not leave laptops visible.

follow_ups.question: How did neighbors react?
follow_ups.response: Mostly with emails, camera clips, and a little overreaction on the neighborhood group.

follow_ups.question: Did it change anything at your house?
follow_ups.response: I set up a better camera angle on the driveway and reminded the kids not to leave bags in the car.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us about experiences of arrest -- of loved ones, family members, friends, or themselves. How about for you?
transcript.response: No arrests for me or immediate family. I had a college acquaintance who got a DUI years ago, but that is about the extent of it.

follow_ups.question: Did that DUI affect your friend group?
follow_ups.response: It made us more serious about designated drivers for a while. We were young enough that some people needed the wake-up call.

follow_ups.question: Any legal issues in your current circle?
follow_ups.response: None that I know of.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they vote in every election, some tell us they don't vote at all. How about you?
transcript.response: I vote regularly, including local elections. I am not someone who puts signs all over the lawn, but I do pay attention to school boards, library funding, infrastructure, and state races. In Michigan, you learn that elections can be close and practical things are on the ballot. Megan and I usually vote absentee now because it fits around work and the kids' schedules. I read local candidate questionnaires more than national cable news.

follow_ups.question: Do you discuss voting choices at home?
follow_ups.response: Yes, but calmly. Megan and I compare notes, especially on school-related offices and ballot proposals.

follow_ups.question: Have you ever skipped an election?
follow_ups.response: Probably a small local election years ago, but in the last decade I have been consistent.

transcript.question_text: How would you describe your political views?
transcript.response: I would call myself a pragmatic center-left independent. I care about competent government, public education, infrastructure, science, and basic fairness. I am not anti-business at all; I work with budgets and know that wishful thinking does not run systems. But I also think markets do not solve everything, especially health care, schools, environmental issues, and poverty. I grew up around auto manufacturing, so I understand why stable jobs, unions, and benefits mattered to families. On social issues I am pretty moderate-to-progressive: I believe people should be treated with dignity, and government should not make private life harder for no good reason. I am skeptical of political extremes and performative outrage. Give me a boring, competent person who reads the brief and fixes the bridge.

follow_ups.question: Which issues matter most to you locally?
follow_ups.response: Schools, roads, library funding, water infrastructure, and responsible zoning. Those are the things you actually feel in daily life.

follow_ups.question: Do you identify with a party?
follow_ups.response: Not strongly. I tend to vote Democratic lately, especially nationally, but I still think of myself as independent.

follow_ups.question: What turns you off politically?
follow_ups.response: Conspiracy thinking, cruelty, and people pretending complicated systems have one-button fixes. That drives me nuts.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about any recent changes in your political views.
transcript.response: I have moved a little more toward institutional reform and public investment than I was in my thirties. Working in technology made me see how fragile systems get when maintenance is deferred, and that maps pretty well onto roads, public health, schools, and government technology. I also became more concerned about misinformation. Ten years ago I thought better information would solve a lot; now I think people also need trust, community, and incentives not to spread nonsense. Having teenagers has made education and online safety feel less abstract.

follow_ups.question: Did the pandemic affect your politics?
follow_ups.response: Yes. It made me value public health competence and clear communication more. It also showed how quickly trust can break down.

follow_ups.question: Have any views moved rightward?
follow_ups.response: Maybe on budgeting discipline. I still want public investment, but I want implementation plans and accountability, not slogans.

transcript.question_text: One topic a lot of people have been talking about recently is race and/or racism and policing. Some tell us issues raised by the Black Lives Matter movement have affected them a lot, some say they've affected them somewhat, others say they haven't affected them at all. How about for you?
transcript.response: They affected me somewhat to a lot, especially because Detroit and the suburbs have such a long racial history. I am a white guy living in Bloomfield Hills, so I have to be honest that my day-to-day experience is insulated. Listening to Black coworkers talk about traffic stops or worrying about teenage sons made it less abstract. I would not say I became an activist, but I paid more attention. It made me think about how policies that seem neutral on paper can land very differently depending on where you live and what you look like.

follow_ups.question: Did you have specific conversations that stayed with you?
follow_ups.response: Yes, a coworker described coaching his son through what to do if stopped by police. I realized I had never had that conversation with Evan in the same way.

follow_ups.question: Did it change anything in your workplace behavior?
follow_ups.response: I tried to listen more in DEI discussions and not jump in with a systems fix before understanding people's experiences.

transcript.question_text: How have you been thinking about the issues Black Lives Matter raises?
transcript.response: I think the core issues are real: unequal treatment, accountability, and whether public safety is being handled in the smartest way. I do not think every slogan captures the operational complexity, but I also do not use complexity as an excuse to dismiss the problem. In my work, when a system creates the same bad outcomes repeatedly, you do root-cause analysis. You do not just blame individual users. That is how I tend to think about policing and race too. Training matters, accountability matters, data matters, and so does the broader economic context.

follow_ups.question: What reforms make sense to you?
follow_ups.response: Better data transparency, stronger accountability for misconduct, mental health response options, and training that is actually measured for outcomes.

follow_ups.question: What concerns you about the debate?
follow_ups.response: People talk past each other. Some dismiss racism entirely, and some ignore practical questions about how emergency response works.

transcript.question_text: How have you been thinking about race in the U.S. recently?
transcript.response: I think race is woven into housing, schools, wealth, policing, and health care in ways that are easy for people like me to overlook because our own lives feel normal to us. Metro Detroit makes that visible if you pay attention: city-suburb divides, school funding differences, property values, and who had access to generational wealth. I do not think guilt is especially useful by itself. Responsibility is more useful. That means supporting fair policies, listening, and being honest with my kids about history rather than pretending everyone started in the same place.

follow_ups.question: How do you talk with your children about it?
follow_ups.response: We talk about local history, housing, schools, and policing when those topics come up. I try not to lecture, but I do not dodge it.

follow_ups.question: Where do you learn about these issues?
follow_ups.response: Local reporting, books, coworkers' perspectives, museum exhibits, and sometimes podcasts. I trust careful reporting more than social media posts.

transcript.question_text: How have you responded to the increased focus on race and/or racism and policing? Some people tell us they're aware of the issue but keep their thoughts to themselves, others say they've talked to family and friends, others have joined protests. What about you?
transcript.response: I have talked with family, friends, and coworkers, donated to a couple local education and legal-aid organizations, and supported some policy changes. I have not joined protests.

follow_ups.question: Why not protests?
follow_ups.response: Partly temperament and partly timing. I am more likely to read, donate, vote, and have direct conversations than be in a crowd.

follow_ups.question: Have those conversations been difficult?
follow_ups.response: Sometimes with older relatives. I try to keep it specific rather than turning it into a cable-news argument.

transcript.question_text: What about people you're close to? How have they responded to the increased focus on race and/or racism and policing?
transcript.response: Megan is probably more engaged than I am because she works with students and families directly. She sees disparities in school resources and student stress up close. My kids are more socially aware than I was at their age, partly because their world is more connected. My parents are sympathetic but sometimes cautious or skeptical about language they hear on the news. My friend group is mixed politically, but most people agree that accountability and fairness should not be controversial.

follow_ups.question: Do political disagreements strain relationships?
follow_ups.response: Occasionally, but not usually beyond repair. I avoid turning every dinner into a debate.

follow_ups.question: Who has influenced you most on this topic?
follow_ups.response: Coworkers and Megan. Hearing lived experience from people I respect carries more weight than pundit arguments.

transcript.question_text: Now we'd like to learn more about your health. First, tell me all about your health.
transcript.response: Overall I would say my health is good, with middle-aged maintenance items. I have mild hypertension that is controlled with medication, and my doctor keeps an eye on cholesterol. I am not an athlete, but I cycle, golf, walk, and try not to sit all weekend. My biggest health risks are stress, screen time, and liking pizza more than a cardiologist would recommend. I sleep decently unless work interrupts it. I am trying to be more consistent rather than dramatic about health.

follow_ups.question: How often do you see a doctor?
follow_ups.response: Annual physical, plus follow-up labs if needed. I am not perfect, but I do go.

follow_ups.question: What medications do you take?
follow_ups.response: A low-dose blood pressure medication. Nothing complicated.

transcript.question_text: For you, what makes it easy or hard to stay healthy?
transcript.response: It is easier because we have good insurance, safe places to exercise, and enough money to buy decent food. It is harder because work can be sedentary and unpredictable. If an outage hits at 4:30, the planned bike ride disappears. Food is also a challenge because I genuinely enjoy cooking rich things like Detroit-style pizza or pork shoulder. I try to balance that with cycling and smaller portions.

follow_ups.question: What healthy habit has stuck best?
follow_ups.response: Sunday rides when weather allows. Having a group helps because I am expected to show up.

follow_ups.question: What habit is hardest?
follow_ups.response: Stopping work at a reasonable hour and not snacking after a long call.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anything big that has happened in the past two years related to your health: any medical diagnoses, flare-ups of chronic conditions, broken bones, pain -- anything like that.
transcript.response: Nothing dramatic. The hypertension diagnosis was a few years ago, but in the last two years my doctor adjusted the dose slightly because my readings crept up during a stressful work period. I also had some lower back stiffness from sitting and from being overconfident moving garage equipment. Physical therapy exercises helped. No broken bones, no hospitalization, no major diagnosis. It was more the usual reminder that being 47 is not the same as being 27.

follow_ups.question: Did the back issue affect your routine?
follow_ups.response: For a few weeks, yes. I skipped golf, stretched more, and raised my monitor setup.

follow_ups.question: What triggered the blood pressure change?
follow_ups.response: A long cloud migration project with late calls, bad sleep, and too much takeout.

transcript.question_text: Sometimes, health problems get in the way. They can even affect people's ability to work or care for their children. How about you?
transcript.response: For me, health has not seriously interfered with work or parenting. A bad back week or poor sleep makes me less patient, but I can still function.

follow_ups.question: Have you taken sick leave recently?
follow_ups.response: A day here and there for a cold or appointments, but nothing extended.

follow_ups.question: Does stress affect your parenting?
follow_ups.response: Yes, if I am not careful. I can get too clipped or distracted, so I try to put the laptop away at dinner.
